idea.title: A reusable 'preserve editorial intent' prompt fragment can reduce, not restore, editorial fidelity
idea.description: Adding a generic editorial-hierarchy instruction to the Narrative prompt (the single change in the candidate) consistently shifted outputs away from the intended company-first message and toward technical orchestration, and it introduced unsupported audience/validation claims — leading to a decision not to promote the change.
idea.audience: Prompt engineers, Narrative/Compose pipeline owners, editorial leads responsible for model-generated messaging
idea.rationale: This experiment provides clear, source-backed evidence that a well-intentioned, reusable prompt fragment — here titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.” — can backfire: candidate runs produced stable, repeatable drift (company identity subordinated, orchestration made central) and added unsupported factual claims. The result matters because it shows that adding high-level generic guidance to a production prompt can worsen, rather than improve, editorial outcomes. Gaps and uncertainty: the result is based on three runs per condition (not statistically conclusive), the model alias may map to different backends over time, and the experiment did not include variant fragment designs or story-specific examples that might behave differently.
idea.evidence: Candidate change: inserted section “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.” (prompt-changes/Narrative.user.prompt.diff). Narrative mean scores dropped from 6.00 to 4.00; Compose mean scores dropped from 5.67 to 3.33. All three candidate Narrative runs and all three candidate Compose runs failed criterion C (orchestration became central) and D (unsupported additions) in every run. Decision: Do not promote; production prompt restored byte-for-byte (rollback SHA-256 matched baseline).

reason: Missed causal attribution and generalization in title, description and rationale.

idea.title: Target the Narrative stage: the most recurrent locus of editorial hierarchy drift
idea.description: Across the recorded runs, the Narrative stage is the most frequent first observable point where a company-first introduction is reframed into a product- or orchestration-centered story. A focused editorial experiment—and upstream-boundary controls—should therefore prioritize validating Narrative inputs and rules before assuming Idea- or Compose-only fixes will succeed.
idea.audience: Product/editorial leads, prompt engineers, experiment designers running the Compose pipeline, and evaluation teams responsible for editorial integrity.
idea.rationale: Why it matters: The report’s cross-experiment analysis shows Narrative is repeatedly the first stage that alters story hierarchy or adds unsupported claims; fixing Narrative behavior promises the highest immediate reduction in downstream reframe/amplification. This gives teams a specific control point to test rules that preserve company-first framing while keeping technical details as support. Gaps and uncertainty: Narrative is the most recurrent but not the sole locus—some runs shift in Idea or Synthesis—so Narrative-focused trials should be designed to detect upstream confounds and include baseline comparisons to Idea/Synthesis inputs.
idea.evidence: Cross-experiment patterns: “Narrative is the most recurrent first visible hierarchy shift.” Specific examples: Experiment 007 candidate runs 001–002 (Narrative first), Experiment 008 A-002 (Narrative factual breach), Experiment 009 baseline 002/003 and candidates 001–003 (Narrative first). The report also notes exceptions where Idea or Synthesis started the drift, so Narrative is frequent but not exclusive.

reason: Missed mandatory Narrative priority and unsupported promise of highest payoff.

idea.title: A useful pilot that couldn’t be evaluated: the museum route lacked outcome measurement
idea.description: The museum created and distributed a printed indoor route for visitors when the sculpture garden flooded, but the pilot recorded distribution (38 copies) and a small operational change (a start sign) while explicitly not tracking whether visitors completed the route or were satisfied. The central point: the experiment produced implementation facts but no outcome data, limiting lessons that can be drawn from the pilot.
idea.audience: Museum operations managers, visitor services teams, front‑of‑house supervisors
idea.rationale: Many museums run small, low‑cost pilots to handle weather or capacity interruptions. This example shows how a simple intervention can be implemented quickly yet leave a critical evaluation gap — useful evidence for teams planning short pilots to include basic measurement (completion, satisfaction) so they can judge effectiveness and iterate responsibly.
idea.evidence: Explicit facts in the source: “the front desk can give visitors a free printed route…”; “In April, the museum handed out the route at two wet Sunday openings. The desk counted 38 copies handed out.” Crucially: “Staff recorded no systematic counts of how many visitors completed the route and did not track visitor satisfaction.” Also: “At the first opening some visitors asked where to start, so a sign was added by the desk at the second.”

reason: Missed explicit visitor purpose replaced by internal pilot evaluation and a measurement agenda.

idea.title: A transparent donor update: explain the limited continuation of the storage trial
idea.description: Tell donors the single, supported story: volunteers ran a six‑month germination check on two retained bean lots in a new dry cupboard; results motivated the committee to continue only those same two lots for another six months and not to expand the trial. The update should present the observed numbers, the committee decision, and explicitly state the trial’s limitations and next step (repeat germination check), without claiming causation or promising garden performance.
idea.audience: Donors and regular supporters of the community seed bank who expect a plain‑spoken status report on funds/activities.
idea.rationale: Why it matters: The source explicitly says a donor update is needed to explain the decision and that the notes give no claim the cupboard caused improvement. A concise, factual update will meet that stated need while avoiding overstated conclusions. Gaps & uncertainty: The source does not record temperature outside the new cupboard, no paired comparison of identical lots was run, different harvest lots were used across years, and no garden‑performance data exist — these limitations should be named in the update so readers understand the evidence boundaries.
idea.evidence: Facts from the source: February germination check — Alder 18/20, Reed 14/20 after six months in new cupboard; previous year’s notebook — Alder 16/20, Reed 15/20 in older room (different harvest lots). Temperature logged only in the new cupboard. Committee decision at March meeting: keep same two lots in cupboard for another six months; has not approved moving other varieties; a volunteer proposed replacing the older room but committee deferred. Source explicitly says no claim that the cupboard caused improvement and no promise of better garden results.

reason: Missed unsupported attribution of committee motivation to the germination results.
provenance: v4 holdout-04-seedbank: exact selected first idea
